name: Pinot Blanc
say: PEE-noh BLAHN, in German VICE-boor-goon-der, in Italian PEE-noh BYAHN-koh

lines.s10: Pinot Blanc is the quiet one of the Pinot family, a gentle dry white of apple, pear and a hint of almond.
lines.s20: Pinot Blanc grows in Alsace, Germany and the north of Italy, where it goes by Weissburgunder or Pinot Bianco. It is a soft, dry white of ripe apple, pear and almond, rounder and milder than most, and a friend to simple food.
lines.s45: Pinot Blanc is the white that never raises its voice. It is the pale member of the Pinot family, grown in Alsace, in Germany as Weissburgunder and in the north of Italy as Pinot Bianco. It tastes of ripe apple, pear and a little almond, and it is dry, soft and medium in body. Most of it is made in steel or old casks, and in Alsace it is the main grape of the sparkling wine. Pour it with quiche, river fish or white asparagus. For generations growers planted it mixed with Chardonnay and took the two for one grape.
lines.sale: Pinot Blanc is the white for a table that cannot agree: soft, dry and mild enough to sit beside almost anything. I would pour it with the lighter fish and the egg dishes, or simply to start.

glass.lead: Ripe apple, pear and white peach with a hint of almond, soft and rounded, on gentle acidity.

ladder.where: Alto Adige's high slopes, Alsace and the Willamette Valley
Baden, the Pfalz and Alto Adige's lower, warmer sites

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium, alcohol moderate, body medium; soft and rounded, a touch fuller where it is raised in cask.

home.home: Alsace, Germany, the north of Italy and Austria. In Alsace it is often blended with Auxerrois and is the main grape of white Crémant d'Alsace. Germany and Austria call it Weissburgunder and make it dry, sometimes in cask. Alto Adige, as Pinot Bianco, grows it high for apple, pear and a sleek, fresh line.
home.abroad: It has travelled little. Oregon's Willamette Valley and California's Central Coast bottle some, mostly in a fresh style that strays little from the quiet model of home.

service.temp: 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius; a cask aged wine a little warmer.
service.glass: A white wine glass; a tulip for Crémant d'Alsace.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary; serve it cool and fresh.
service.age: Enjoy it young, within two to four years; a few cask aged wines keep longer.

with.why: soft fruit and gentle acidity suit eggs and cream
a mild wine that does not fight the asparagus
gentle fruit and no new oak beside delicate fish
a rounded body matches white meat

labels.means: The German and Austrian name, white Burgundian; dry as a rule.
The Italian name, met above all from Alto Adige and Friuli.
An old Alsace name for Pinot Blanc, still seen on some labels.
Alsace's bottle fermented sparkling wine; Pinot Blanc is the main grape of the white.

guest.q: Is Pinot Blanc like Pinot Grigio?
guest.a: They are kin in the Pinot family. Pinot Blanc is softer and rounder, with ripe apple and almond; Italian Pinot Grigio is usually lighter, crisper and more neutral.

guest.q: I like Chardonnay but not the oak. Would this suit me?
guest.a: It may well. Pinot Blanc has a similar rounded feel and apple fruit, but it is milder and is seldom put in new oak.
It is the German and Austrian name for Pinot Blanc: the same grape, usually made dry, with apple, pear and a hint of almond.

compare.tell: Chardonnay has more body and a firmer line, and often cream or toast from the cellar; Pinot Blanc is milder and softer, with apple and almond.
Pinot Gris from Alsace is richer and oilier, with spiced pear and a faint bitterness; Pinot Blanc is lighter, plainer and fresher.
Aligoté is sharper and more lemony, with higher acidity; Pinot Blanc is softer and rounder, with ripe apple and almond.

profile.st: Pale lemon · Body medium · Acid medium · Alcohol moderate · Dry; also the base of Crémant d'Alsace
profile.fruit: Ripe apple, pear and quince, white peach; lemon and lemon zest from high, cool sites
profile.other: Almond, hazelnut and green walnut, apple blossom, acacia blossom; bread dough with age or in sparkling wine; seldom any new oak
profile.tell: Soft, round and mild: apple, pear and almond on gentle acidity with no loud perfume, a quieter, lighter wine than Chardonnay
profile.regions: Alsace (often with Auxerrois, and in Crémant d'Alsace), Germany and Austria (Weissburgunder), Alto Adige and Friuli (Pinot Bianco), Willamette Valley
profile.confuse: Chardonnay has more body and often cream or toast; Pinot Gris is richer and oilier, with spiced pear; Aligoté is sharper and more lemony

cards.front: Pinot Blanc: its German and Italian names, and its family?
cards.back: Weissburgunder in Germany and Austria, Pinot Bianco in Italy. It is a white berried mutation within the Pinot family, kin to Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris.

cards.front: What part does Pinot Blanc play in Alsace?
cards.back: It makes a soft, dry white, often blended with Auxerrois and sold as Pinot Blanc, and it is the main grape of white Crémant d'Alsace.

cards.front: Pinot Blanc in the glass: what gives it away?
cards.back: Ripe apple, pear and almond, a soft, rounded feel and gentle acidity, with no loud perfume and seldom any new oak: a quieter, lighter wine than Chardonnay.

questions.q: A German list offers a dry white called Weissburgunder from Baden. A guest asks which grape that is. What do you answer?
questions.exp: Weissburgunder, white Burgundian, is the German name for Pinot Blanc. Pinot Gris is Grauburgunder in German, and Chardonnay and Silvaner are sold under their own names.

questions.q: A blind white is pale and dry, with ripe apple, pear and a hint of almond, a soft, rounded feel, gentle acidity and no trace of a barrel. Which grape fits it?
questions.exp: Soft apple, pear and almond on gentle acidity with no loud perfume points to Pinot Blanc. Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling have far sharper acidity, and Gewürztraminer smells of lychee and rose petal.

questions.q: A guest enjoys her glass of white Crémant d'Alsace and asks which grape leads most of it. Which do you name?
questions.exp: Pinot Blanc is the main grape of white Crémant d'Alsace, chosen for its freshness and soft fruit. Riesling, Gewürztraminer and Muscat are Alsace's aromatic grapes, met mostly as still wines under their own names.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it; a thin grape, so it carries its profile. The Régionale row reads true and nothing here departs from it.

The parentage is worded as a white berried mutation within the Pinot family: the German and Austrian wine bodies say a mutation of Pinot Gris, the Davis grape book an independent mutation of Pinot Noir.

The closing line, that growers long planted it mixed with Chardonnay and took the two for one, stands on the Davis grape book and on the Alto Adige body's variety fact sheet, which dates the separate description of Chardonnay to 1872.

Abroad names the Willamette Valley and the Central Coast, which the Codex's own region records already name for the grape. The Oregon Wine Board and Wines of British Columbia pages also support Oregon and British Columbia; they are not listed for the cap of four sources, and British Columbia is left out of the text.
Left out: Klevener de Heiligenstein as a different grape from Klevner, and the list of grapes Crémant d'Alsace permits, for want of a source read in this session.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after four fixes. Alsace, Auxerrois, Klevner and the place of the grape in Crémant d'Alsace were confirmed.
changed: glass.notes, the ladder and the profile: hay flowers becomes acacia blossom, and grapefruit and lime become lemon zest. A study of Austrian Pinot Blanc gives pear, apple, walnut and a hint of acacia flower; hay is the mark of Silvaner in that grape's tell against this one, and no source gives grapefruit or lime.
glass.ladder, the moderate rung: Alto Adige's warm valley floors becomes its lower, warmer sites. The grape is grown there on slopes from about 250 to 900 metres.
worlds.home.abroad: mostly is added, since some California bottles are rounder than the model of home.
guest, the third answer: a faint nutty note, a family word in disguise, becomes a hint of almond.
open: The parentage is left as the author worded it, a white berried mutation within the Pinot family: the sources split between a mutation of Pinot Gris and one of Pinot Noir.
